intro: Email bounce rate is the share of sent emails that were rejected outright rather than accepted. Enter emails sent and bounced to get the rate.

sections.heading: How Email Bounce Rate is calculated
sections.body: Bounce Rate = Bounced Emails ÷ Emails Sent — [the same bounced-over-sent shape Mailtrap uses to define email bounce rate](https://www.mailtrap.io/blog/email-bounce-rate/). Sent, not delivered, is the denominator here: a bounced email is being measured against everything that was attempted, since bouncing is what determines whether a send ever became a delivery in the first place.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: 150 ÷ 10,000 = 1.50%. This is a blended figure covering every bounced email — whether the address didn't exist at all or the recipient's inbox happened to be full that day, both count the same way here.

sections.heading: A blended bounce rate hides hard vs. soft bounces
sections.body: [A hard bounce is a permanent delivery failure — an invalid address, a nonexistent domain — while a soft bounce is a temporary issue, like a full inbox or a server that was briefly down](https://www.mailtrap.io/blog/email-bounce-rate/). The two mean very different things for list health: hard bounces should be removed from a list immediately and signal genuine list-hygiene problems, while soft bounces are often self-resolving and don't carry the same reputation risk. This calculator computes one blended rate from total bounces; if the input distinguishes hard from soft, reporting them separately reveals a real signal a combined number hides.

sections.heading: Email Bounce Rate is not Web Bounce Rate
sections.body: These share a name but measure completely unrelated things. Email bounce rate is about delivery failure — a message that was rejected before it ever reached an inbox. Web bounce rate (a legacy web-analytics concept, since replaced by engagement rate in GA4) was about visitor behavior — someone landing on a page and leaving without further interaction, a message that was successfully delivered and seen. Confusing the two isn't just imprecise language; they're computed from entirely different systems and denominators, and neither number says anything about the other.

faq.a: Email bounce rate is the percentage of sent emails that were rejected and never delivered, calculated as bounced emails divided by total emails sent. It's specifically about delivery failure — an invalid address, a full inbox, a server issue — not about how recipients behaved after receiving a message. This is a different metric from "bounce rate" in web analytics, which historically measured single-page website visits, a concept GA4 has since replaced with engagement rate. Email bounce rate and web bounce rate share a name but are computed from entirely unrelated systems and mean nothing about each other. Keeping email bounce rate low is a direct sender-reputation concern, since mailbox providers track it when deciding how much trust to extend a given sender.

faq.q: How do you calculate Email Bounce Rate?
faq.a: Divide bounced emails by emails sent: Bounce Rate = Bounced ÷ Sent. A campaign that sent 10,000 emails with 150 bounces has a bounce rate of 150 ÷ 10,000 = 1.50%. Both numbers need to come from the same send and reporting window, and bounced emails should never exceed the sent count, since every bounce started as a send attempt. If a hard-bounce and soft-bounce breakdown is available, computing separate rates for each reveals more than a single blended figure, since the two types carry very different implications for list health. Most email service providers calculate and report this figure automatically in campaign analytics, breaking bounces down by type in more detailed reporting views.

faq.q: What's the difference between a hard bounce and a soft bounce?
faq.a: A hard bounce is a permanent failure — the email address doesn't exist, the domain is invalid, or the message was blocked outright — and it should typically be removed from a mailing list right away, since repeated hard bounces damage sender reputation. A soft bounce is a temporary issue, like a full inbox or a recipient's server being briefly unavailable, and often resolves on its own without list action. A blended bounce rate treats both the same way, which can hide a genuine list-hygiene problem behind what looks like a normal, low overall number if the mix happens to lean soft.
